articles.title: Lawyer Isn’t Close To The Most Impressive Thing On His Résumé
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Since the National Baseball Hall of Fame opened in 1936, it has enshrined roughly 346 players, managers, executives, and commissioners — and, by a recent tally, 11 of them were also lawyers. Who is the Hall of Fame manager with three World Series rings who picked up a law degree and bar admission along the way, even though he never hung out a shingle?

Hint: He won it all with the Oakland A’s and the St. Louis Cardinals, earned his law degree at Florida State, and in 2009, briefly made legal headlines of his own by suing Twitter over a fake account using his name.

See the answer on the next page.

The post Lawyer Isn’t Close To The Most Impressive Thing On His Résumé appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Sun Through The Clouds
articles.content:
There is a good reason it has been a month since my previous column. I am coming off one of the great adventures of my professional career: a trip to Tokyo as a co-host of the first-ever Patent Monetization Symposium. Thankfully, to say the event was a success would be an understatement on many levels. Considering the quality of the attendees and my co-presenters, however, that success should not be a surprise. On both an individual and collective basis, everyone was there to educate or to learn about current best practices and approaches to patent monetization, with a particular focus on the opportunities and challenges facing Japanese technology companies and investors active in the Japanese market. And the connection between presenters and attendees was established, with two hours of discussion and Q & A to a full room of interested high-level IP and investment professionals, followed by a cocktail hour in one of Tokyo’s most iconic venues.
As thankful as I am to our co-hosts, my partner, each of the presenters that joined us, our sponsors, and most of all the attendees, I am even more thankful for the upcoming chance to help shape the ongoing story of Japanese innovation. For over a decade, a big part of our practice has been monetizing patents sourced from Japanese technology leaders, but even that direct experience is just enough to tease an appreciation for what lies ahead. And how could it be otherwise, when even our Zoom-driven efforts to globalize our practice is just a pale substitute for getting on a plane and visiting potential business counterparts in person. Besides demonstrating respect and commitment to the effort, travel has a way of fostering creativity and enthusiasm on the part of the traveler in a way that can be very energizing. There is something invigorating about changing one’s perspective by getting out of one’s usual workflow and environment, especially when one is aiming to take on a significant challenge in the pursuit of growth.
(Before I get into some of what was learned about the state of innovation in Japan today, it is important to share some more general thoughts about mental and physical health. International travel is taxing, even when one gives consideration to flight schedules and dealing with jet lag on both ends of the trip. As important as it can be to think expansively about pursuing opportunities outside of our routine, it would be a mistake to discount the physical and mental strain of doing so. At the same time, attention to mental and physical health can be a potent spur for creative thinking and a willingness to tackle new adventures. Accordingly, this is as good a time as any — especially as the holiday season approaches –- for all of us to take stock of our routines and how we are treating our mind and body. For those interested, I am enjoying Andrew Huberman’s new book, which I find has many good ideas for busy lawyers to consider.)
While there may be tougher briefs than visiting a world-class city like Tokyo, when it comes to considering the IP position of many Japanese technology companies large and small, the challenge is a sobering one. On the one hand, many of these companies have proud histories of innovation -– and based on what we heard from numerous attendees, remain as motivated as ever to contribute to the world through the genius and creativity of their engineers and employees. Propelled by that driving force, as well as the significant financial resources that the Japanese investment community and government can bring to bear, the future is bright for Japanese innovation. On the other hand, many of those same companies are facing pressure to contain their spending, particularly with respect to maintenance fees on patent portfolios not tied to core ongoing business objectives. But cost-savings may not be enough to allow those companies to reach their goals for continued innovation, hence the interest in learning about patent monetization opportunities that may be available. Judging by the level of interest we saw in our presentation, as well as the quality of questions we received, the audience was paying attention.
With good reason, at least in my view. For one, how else would they get such direct exposure to all the different entities that underlie professional patent monetization today? Trial lawyers, insurance brokers, funders, damages experts and professional monetization managers all in one room, discussing a mock transaction from patent identification to acquisition to deployment to economic recoveries. Without living through the process, it can be hard to develop an appreciation for how much intellectual horsepower and diligence effort is needed to develop a single successful transaction. Seeing everyone involved on one stage underscored for the audience — and was a potent personal reminder — of how important solid working relationships are in the service of moving worthwhile deals along. (Defendants may not yet have developed that level of appreciation, but I think our audience did.) Furthermore, we tried to communicate that the macro environment for patent monetization is as good as it has been in recent memory. That fact, coupled with the immediate pressure on Japanese companies to make something out of their investment in their patent portfolios, should engender a lot of follow up discussions in the days ahead.
Ultimately, the success of any business development exercise is felt on a number of levels. First, when done right, the experience helps cement existing relationships and fosters a willingness to explore ways to deepen collaboration over time. Second, preparing for and presenting to others on the state of play in a given market has a way of sharpening one’s thinking about where the true opportunities lie — and where energies should be invested most wisely going forward. And lastly, there is a tangible boost in focus and commitment that arises when a new adventure is being embarked on. Helping Japanese companies rediscover the sun through the clouds when it comes to patent management is a task bigger than any one person or group. But I look forward to doing my part.
Please feel free to send comments or questions to me at gaston@k2k.law or via Twitter: @gkroub. Any topic suggestions or thoughts are most welcome.
Gaston Kroub lives in Brooklyn and is a founding partner of K2K IP Law, an intellectual property litigation boutique that also serves as a leading consultancy on patent issues for the investment community. Gaston’s practice focuses on intellectual property litigation and related counseling, with a strong focus on patent matters. You can reach him at gaston@k2k.law or follow him on Twitter: @gkroub.

articles.title: Reports Of The Billable Hour’s Demise Are Greatly Exaggerated, 8am Data Finds
articles.content:
Reports of the demise of the billable hour have been greatly exaggerated, at least at smaller law firms.
With apologies to Mark Twain, that is the central finding of a new report on billing and payment practices at small and midsized law firms. It finds that firms billing solely by the hour outnumber firms billing solely by flat fee by nearly 5 to 1, and that flat fees, far from gaining ground over the past year, actually lost a little.
The 8am SMB Law Billing and Payments Report, released today by 8am, the company formerly known as AffiniPay, analyzes aggregate billing and payment data from more than 60,000 law firms, predominantly in the U.S., that use its MyCase practice management and LawPay payments platforms.
It compares the first half of 2026 against the first half of 2025, and the company says it will publish the report twice a year going forward.
The report says it defines firm size by employee count, with a solo being one, small being 2-5, medium being 6-10, and large being 11 or more. That number is derived from either firm-reported data when available or platform user counts where not. The report does not break down how many of the 60,000 law firms fall into each category.
“For most of the past decade, the legal industry has been predicting a shift away from the billable hour, because clients want predictability,” the report says. “The data showed firms making a different choice.”
Of firms covered by the report, 47.7% billed entirely by the hour in the first half of 2026, up from 46.6% a year earlier. Just 10.3% billed exclusively by flat fee, up from 9.7%. The remaining 42% used a mix, but even they used flat fees in just a quarter or fewer of their invoices.
Measured by invoices rather than firms, flat fees made up 15% of all bills sent in the first half of 2026, down from 16% a year earlier. Large firms cut back the most, from about 16% to 14%. Solo firms were the exception, inching up to 17%.
“Flat fee trends are a prime example – the industry narrative suggests many are moving in that direction, but our data shows most SMB firms have not,” said Tanya Hendricks, chief product officer at 8am, in a statement. “All too often, firms are making consequential decisions about how they bill and receive payments without real benchmarks to measure against.”
The Practice Determines the Billing Method
Where flat fees have taken hold, it is because of the nature of the work, not a change in philosophy, the report says. Flat fees accounted for 87.7% of invoices at traffic firms and 64% at immigration firms, both practice areas built on routine, bounded matters. Bankruptcy and criminal defense firms each sent about half their bills as flat fees.
At the other end of the spectrum, flat fees made up 10% of invoices at business and corporate firms, 6.7% in civil litigation, 2.8% in family law and 0.8% in workers’ compensation.
Notably, immigration, even though it is one of the practice areas most likely to use flat fees, saw its flat-fee share drop more than four points, from 68.4% to 64%.
“Billing model is largely determined by the work, not preference,” the report says. “Before choosing between flat fee and hourly, consider whether a given matter is predictable and bounded enough to price up front. If it is, a flat fee makes sense. If it isn’t, hourly protects the firm.”
Billings Rose, But Not Rates
Beyond how firms structured their fees, the report finds that firms grew their monthly billings by 5% to 8% over the year.
That was not the result of raising rates, as the report finds that hourly rates were unchanged at three of the four firm sizes the report tracked, with only medium firms having raised their rates by 4.3%.
Instead, the report attributes the growth to realization, finding that more of the time firms were already recording made it onto an invoice.
Large firms billed nearly 12% more hours while logging slightly fewer, raising the share of recorded hours they billed from 44% to 49%. The amount firms earned per hour billed rose between 3% and 5% across all sizes.
Solo firms went the other way. Their recorded hours rose nearly 9%, but the share they billed slipped from 70% to 69%.
“Before raising rates, assess how much tracked time is being invoiced,” the report advises.
Payments Become More Reliable
On the payments side, the report has good news for firms. Every month in the first half of 2026 outperformed the same month in 2025, across all firm sizes. The report finds:
- Invoices paid within 30 days rose from 57.7% to 59.1%.
- Invoices overdue at 30 days fell from 26.8% to 25.6%.
- The share of invoiced dollars collected within 30 days rose from 43.4% to 45.1%.
- The average unpaid balance per invoice fell from $2,073 to $1,979.
Even so, roughly seven in 10 firms were still carrying at least one past-due invoice, which was the same as the prior year. “Less money is outstanding,” the report says, “but the number of firms carrying outstanding balances did not change.”
Solo practitioners had the lowest overdue rate, at 18.8%, compared with 26.8% at small firms, 27% at medium firms and 24.1% at large firms.
The speed at which payments were made varied by practice area. Traffic firms were the most likely to have an invoice paid in full within a month (77.2%), followed by estate planning (68.1%) and real estate (65.5%).
Workers’ compensation firms were the least likely (33.8%), but they also had the fewest overdue invoices of any practice area (8%), because insurers pay on longer but more predictable schedules.
Family law had the highest overdue rate, at 32%. Debt-collection firms improved the most, cutting their overdue rate by almost nine percentage points.
The Cost of Getting Paid
The report also finds that firms are becoming more deliberate about what it costs them to accept payment. The number of firms adding a surcharge to card payments rose 16% year over year, while the surcharge rate itself held steady at about 2.6%. On average, firms collected 25% more in surcharges than a year earlier.
Firms also steered larger payments toward e-check, which is priced per transaction rather than as a percentage. The average e-check payment was $2,206, compared with $1,491 for card payments, and card payments’ share of dollars collected fell about two percentage points.
Large firms led the way on both fronts, which the report attributes to their larger average payments — $2,231 per transaction, versus $1,503 at solo firms — making percentage-based card fees costlier for them.
Small firms, by contrast, moved in the opposite direction, offering clients flexibility such as pay-later options rather than pushing costs onto them. The report notes that firms should check their state’s rules before surcharging, since some jurisdictions prohibit it.
“The picture that is emerging is one of firms getting more disciplined: getting paid more reliably, billing more of what they’ve already earned, and making more deliberate choices about how they get paid,” Hendricks said.
A Focus on Smaller Firms
The report makes clear that the findings solely reflect 8am’s own customer base. “Data reflects the activity of 8am users and is not representative of every law firm in the U.S. legal market,” it says.
That means that the data skews towards toward solo and small firms in consumer-facing practice areas.
The company says it compared the same firms across both periods, weighted each firm equally in the payment figures, counted invoices as paid or overdue against a 30-day window, and excluded test accounts, trial accounts, draft invoices and inactive firms.
That said, 60,000 firms are a large sample, and the report is based on actual invoices rather than self-reporting.
Its finding that small firms are not abandoning the billable hour is consistent with what other industry surveys continue to show – and underscores that the billable hour, despite reports to the contrary, remains alive and well.

articles.title: Weil’s Successor Walked Away, And Now The Firm Has A ‘Run On The Bank’ Problem
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
The very fact that she declined to step up would signal to any partner with their head screwed on that she has lost faith. And what I’m afraid is going to happen is the run on the bank psychology, which all too often we have seen means the end for law firms.
— Bruce MacEwen, a law firm consultant at Adam Smith, Esq., warning Bloomberg Law that Ramona Nee’s decision to turn down the executive-partner role could further unsettle Weil Gotshal’s partnership. Nee was slated to succeed Barry Wolf in January, but her withdrawal leaves the firm without a clear successor as it faces mounting partner departures and failed merger talks. Wolf had described a smooth handoff as his priority, saying in May, “Nothing would make me happier or prouder than her leading this firm to even greater heights.”
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
